lessons.title: Common Onion Pests: Thrips, Onion Maggot, and Nematodes
lessons.body:
Thrips are tiny, slender insects about 1-2 mm long. They feed by sucking sap from onion leaves, causing silvery streaks and curled tips. In Africa, the onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) is most common. Scout by shaking plants over a white sheet of paper; if you see 10 or more thrips per plant, treat. Use yellow sticky traps (10 traps per acre) to monitor. Spray with neem oil (3 ml per litre of water) every 7 days, or use insecticidal soap. For severe cases, apply imidacloprid (0.5 ml per litre) but rotate with other chemicals to avoid resistance.

Onion maggot (Delia antiqua) larvae tunnel into bulbs, causing wilting and rot. Adults are small grey flies that lay eggs near the base of plants. Prevent by rotating cropsâdon't plant onions where onions or related crops grew in the last 3 years. Use row covers (fine mesh) immediately after planting. Apply beneficial nematodes (Steinernema feltiae) to soil at 1 million per square metre. If maggots appear, drench soil with spinosad (1 ml per litre) around plant bases.

Nematodes are microscopic worms that attack roots, causing stunted growth and yellowing. Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.) are common in sandy soils. Test soil before planting: take 20 soil cores per acre, mix, and send to a lab. If nematodes are present, solarize soil by covering with clear plastic for 6 weeks during hot season. Plant marigolds (Tagetes erecta) as a cover cropâthey release compounds that kill nematodes. Apply neem cake (200 g per square metre) before planting. Chemical nematicides like fenamiphos are dangerous; use only as last resort with protective gear.

Always inspect your crop twice a week. Early detection saves harvest. Keep records of pest sightings to plan rotations and treatments.

lessons.title: Common Diseases: Downy Mildew, Botrytis, and Purple Blotch
lessons.body:
Downy mildew (Peronospora destructor) appears as pale, elongated patches on leaves, often with a fuzzy grey-purple growth on the underside. It spreads fast in cool, humid weather (15-22Â°C) with leaf wetness. To control, plant resistant varieties like 'Red Creole' or 'Texas Grano'. Space plants 10-15 cm apart for airflow. Water early in the day so leaves dry before evening. If symptoms appear, spray with copper oxychloride (3 g per litre) every 10 days. Remove and burn infected leaves. In severe cases, use metalaxyl (2 g per litre) but rotate with copper to prevent resistance.

Botrytis leaf blight and neck rot (Botrytis squamosa and B. allii) cause white spots on leaves and soft rot in bulbs during storage. The fungus survives in soil and crop debris. Practice 3-year rotation with cereals. Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation. Harvest when necks are dry and tops fall over. Cure bulbs in a warm, dry, ventilated area for 2-3 weeks. Store at 0-4Â°C with low humidity. If botrytis appears in field, spray with iprodione (2 ml per litre) or Bacillus subtilis (5 g per litre) every 7-10 days. Remove infected plants immediately.

Purple blotch (Alternaria porri) causes small white spots that enlarge into purple lesions with concentric rings. It thrives in warm, wet conditions (25-30Â°C). Use certified disease-free seed. Treat seeds with hot water at 50Â°C for 20 minutes before planting. Apply potassium bicarbonate (5 g per litre) weekly as a preventive. For active infection, spray with mancozeb (2.5 g per litre) or chlorothalonil (2 g per litre) every 7 days. Alternate chemicals to avoid resistance. Remove crop debris after harvest and burn it.

Always wear gloves and a mask when handling fungicides. Keep a field diary to track disease outbreaks and treatments.

lessons.title: Scouting and Monitoring Techniques
lessons.body:
Scouting means walking your onion field regularly to check for pests and diseases. Do it at least twice a week, early morning or late afternoon when pests are active. Use a systematic pattern: walk in a zigzag or 'W' shape across the field, stopping at 10 random spots per acre. At each spot, inspect 5 plants. Look at leaves, stems, and soil around the base. Carry a hand lens (10x magnification) to see tiny pests like thrips. Also bring a notebook, a white sheet of paper, and a small trowel.

For thrips, shake a plant over white paper and count the insects. Threshold: treat if you find 10 or more thrips per plant. For onion maggot, look for wilting plants and dig around the base to find larvae or pupae. For nematodes, check roots for galls or swellingsâdig up a few plants and examine roots. For diseases, note leaf spots, fuzzy growth, or wilting. Take photos with your phone for records. Use yellow sticky traps (10 per acre) and pheromone traps for moths. Check traps weekly and count catches.

Keep a scouting log with date, location, pest/disease found, and severity (low, medium, high). This helps you decide when to act. For example, if you see downy mildew on 5% of plants, spray copper immediately. If you see only 1-2 thrips per plant, wait and monitor. Share your log with other farmers to track regional outbreaks. Use a smartphone app like 'Plantix' to identify diseases from photos.

Set action thresholds: thripsâ10 per plant; downy mildewâany sign; botrytisâfirst spots; purple blotchâfirst lesions. Train a worker to scout when you are away. Remember, early detection reduces pesticide use and saves money. Clean your tools and boots between fields to avoid spreading pathogens.

lessons.title: Biological and Cultural Control Methods
lessons.body:
Biological control uses living organisms to manage pests. For thrips, release predatory mites (Amblyseius cucumeris) at 100 mites per square metre every 2 weeks. Ladybugs (Coccinella septempunctata) eat aphids and thripsâattract them by planting sunflowers or dill nearby. For onion maggot, apply beneficial nematodes (Steinernema feltiae) to soil at 1 million per square metre. For nematodes, grow marigolds (Tagetes spp.) as a cover crop before onions; their roots release a compound that kills nematodes. Also, spray Bacillus subtilis (5 g per litre) for botrytis and purple blotch. These methods are safe for you and the environment.

Cultural control means changing how you farm to prevent pests. Rotate crops: never plant onions after onions, garlic, or leeks for at least 3 years. Plant cereals like maize or sorghum in between. Use certified disease-free seeds and treat them with hot water (50Â°C for 20 minutes) before sowing. Space plants 10-15 cm apart to improve airflow and reduce humidity. Water early in the day with drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers. Remove and burn crop debris after harvest. Solarize soil by covering with clear plastic for 6 weeks in hot season to kill nematodes and fungi.

Plant resistant varieties: 'Red Creole' resists downy mildew; 'Texas Grano' tolerates purple blotch. Use row covers (fine mesh) to keep out onion maggot flies. Mulch with straw to reduce soil splash and weed growth. Encourage natural enemies by planting border crops like marigolds and coriander. Keep field clean: remove weeds that host pests. Store bulbs properly: cure for 2-3 weeks in dry, ventilated shade, then store at 0-4Â°C.

Combine these methods for best results. For example, rotate crops, use row covers, and release beneficial insects. This reduces chemical use and builds a healthy farm. Always observe your field to see what works.

lessons.title: Chemical Control: Safe Pesticide Use
lessons.body:
Chemical pesticides can control severe pest outbreaks, but they must be used safely. Always read the label before buying. Choose pesticides registered for onions, like imidacloprid for thrips, spinosad for maggots, copper oxychloride for downy mildew, and mancozeb for purple blotch. Buy from reputable agro-dealers and check expiry dates. Never use banned chemicals like DDT or lindane. Store pesticides in a locked cabinet away from children, food, and animals.

Wear protective gear: gloves, long-sleeved shirt, trousers, boots, goggles, and a face mask. Mix chemicals outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. Use clean water and measure accurately with a measuring cupânever guess. For example, mix 0.5 ml imidacloprid per litre of water for thrips. Spray early morning or late evening when bees are not active. Avoid spraying on windy days or before rain. Use a calibrated knapsack sprayer; rinse it three times after use and spray the rinse water on a non-crop area.

Follow pre-harvest intervals (PHI): imidaclopridâ7 days; spinosadâ3 days; copperâ1 day; mancozebâ7 days. Do not harvest before PHI or you risk pesticide residues. Rotate chemicals with different modes of action to prevent resistance. For example, alternate imidacloprid with spinosad every 10 days. Never mix more than two chemicals unless the label says it's safe. Keep a record of spray dates, chemicals, and rates.

Dispose of empty containers by triple-rinsing and puncturing them, then bury or take to a collection point. Never reuse pesticide containers. If you feel dizzy or sick after spraying, move to fresh air and seek medical help. Teach workers about safety. Remember, chemicals are a last resortâuse them only when scouting shows thresholds are exceeded.

lessons.title: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) Plan
lessons.body:
An IPM plan combines all methodsâscouting, cultural, biological, and chemicalâto manage pests with minimal harm. Start by scouting twice a week. Keep a log. Set action thresholds: thripsâ10 per plant; downy mildewâany sign; botrytisâfirst spots; purple blotchâfirst lesions. When threshold is reached, act. First, try cultural and biological controls. For example, if thrips are at 8 per plant, release predatory mites and spray neem oil. Only if they exceed 10, use imidacloprid. This saves money and protects beneficial insects.

Create a year-round plan. Before planting: test soil for nematodes, solarize if needed, and choose resistant varieties. Plant certified seed treated with hot water. Space plants 10-15 cm apart. Use drip irrigation and mulch. During growth: scout regularly, remove infected plants, and apply biocontrols. If disease appears, spray copper or Bacillus subtilis. After harvest: remove and burn debris, rotate to a cereal crop, and store bulbs properly. Keep records of every action.

Work with neighbors to manage pests regionally. If everyone rotates crops and destroys debris, pest pressure drops. Attend training sessions and share knowledge. Use smartphone apps like 'Plantix' for diagnosis. Set aside a small budget for biocontrols and safe chemicals. For a 1-acre onion field, an IPM plan might cost: neem oil (500 ml) â $10; predatory mites â $20; copper fungicide â $15; sticky traps â $5. Total $50, much less than weekly chemical sprays.

Review your plan each season. What worked? What didn't? Adjust. For example, if thrips were severe, plant more marigolds next time. IPM is flexible and site-specific. It protects your health, the environment, and your profits. Start small, be consistent, and teach others.

quiz.q: What is the recommended action threshold for thrips per onion plant?
quiz.explanation: Treat when you find 10 or more thrips per plant to prevent economic damage.

quiz.q: Which pest tunnels into onion bulbs causing rot?
quiz.explanation: Onion maggot larvae bore into bulbs, leading to wilting and decay.

quiz.q: What is a good cultural control for nematodes?
quiz.explanation: Marigolds release compounds that suppress nematodes in the soil.

quiz.q: Which disease causes fuzzy grey-purple growth on leaf undersides?
quiz.explanation: Downy mildew is identified by fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves.

quiz.q: What is the hot water treatment temperature for onion seeds?
quiz.explanation: Soaking seeds at 50Â°C for 20 minutes kills seed-borne pathogens.

quiz.q: Which fungicide is recommended for purple blotch?
quiz.explanation: Mancozeb is effective against Alternaria porri, the cause of purple blotch.

quiz.q: How often should you scout your onion field?
quiz.explanation: Scouting twice a week helps detect pests and diseases early.

quiz.q: What tool is useful for seeing tiny pests like thrips?
quiz.explanation: A 10x hand lens allows you to see thrips and other small pests.

quiz.q: Which biological control agent can be released for thrips?
quiz.explanation: Predatory mites like Amblyseius cucumeris feed on thrips.

quiz.q: What is the pre-harvest interval (PHI) for imidacloprid on onions?
quiz.explanation: Wait 7 days after spraying imidacloprid before harvesting.

quiz.q: Which practice helps prevent onion maggot?
quiz.explanation: Rotating away from onions for 3 years breaks the maggot life cycle.

quiz.q: What is a sign of nematode damage on onion roots?
quiz.explanation: Root-knot nematodes cause galls or swellings on roots.

quiz.q: Which method is used to solarize soil?
quiz.explanation: Clear plastic traps heat to kill soil-borne pests and pathogens.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for onion plants to reduce disease?
quiz.explanation: Spacing plants 10-15 cm apart improves airflow and reduces humidity.

quiz.q: Which chemical is used for downy mildew?
quiz.explanation: Copper oxychloride is effective against downy mildew.

quiz.q: What should you wear when applying pesticides?
quiz.explanation: Protective gear prevents pesticide poisoning.

quiz.q: How many yellow sticky traps per acre are recommended for monitoring?
quiz.explanation: 10 traps per acre help monitor thrips and other flying pests.

quiz.q: Which disease causes soft rot in stored onions?
quiz.explanation: Botrytis neck rot leads to soft rot during storage.

quiz.q: What is the first step in an IPM plan?
quiz.explanation: Scouting identifies pest levels and guides decisions.

quiz.q: Which biological fungicide can control botrytis?
quiz.explanation: Bacillus subtilis is a biofungicide effective against botrytis.

quiz.q: What is the action threshold for downy mildew?
quiz.explanation: Any sign of downy mildew requires immediate treatment.

quiz.q: Which crop is a good rotation partner for onions?
quiz.explanation: Maize is a cereal and does not host onion pests.

quiz.q: How long should you solarize soil to kill nematodes?
quiz.explanation: 6 weeks of solarization in hot weather reduces nematode populations.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to dispose of pesticide containers?
quiz.explanation: Triple-rinsing and burying prevents environmental contamination.

quiz.q: Which beneficial insect eats thrips?
quiz.explanation: Ladybugs are predators of thrips and other soft-bodied pests.

quiz.q: What is the PHI for spinosad?
quiz.explanation: Wait 3 days after applying spinosad before harvest.

quiz.q: Which disease shows concentric rings on lesions?
quiz.explanation: Purple blotch lesions have distinct concentric rings.

quiz.q: What is a good way to attract beneficial insects?
quiz.explanation: Sunflowers and dill attract ladybugs and other predators.

quiz.q: How often should you rotate chemicals to prevent resistance?
quiz.explanation: Rotate chemicals with different modes of action every 10 days.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do if you feel dizzy after spraying?
quiz.explanation: Move to fresh air immediately and seek medical help if needed.
